fixes.answer: In my view, lasting happiness comes primarily [[from within]] and from our connections, rather than from external possessions. Strong, loving relationships seem to be the greatest source of happiness. Beyond that, having a sense of purpose, good health, and the freedom to pursue what we find meaningful all contribute enormously. So I believe true happiness is [[rooted in]] connection, purpose and [[gratitude]], not in material wealth.
fixes.why: 'connection' and 'purpose' are plain; marked 'from within' and 'rooted in'; softened 'consistently shown'

fixes.answer: This is a fascinating and debated question. In material terms, we are far better off than previous generations, with more comfort, health and opportunity. Yet, [[curiously]], rates of anxiety and depression seem to be rising, especially among the young. It appears that material progress has not straightforwardly translated into greater happiness. So while we have gained much, I am not convinced we are [[fundamentally]] happier, which suggests happiness depends on more than mere [[prosperity]] and comfort.
fixes.why: only 2 marks and 'comfort' is plain; marked sir's 'fundamentally' and 'curiously'

fixes.answer: This reflects the fact that money, beyond meeting basic needs, has [[diminishing returns]] on happiness. Wealthy people may still suffer from poor relationships, a lack of purpose, or the isolation and pressure that wealth can bring. There is also the phenomenon where people constantly adapt and want more, never feeling satisfied. So it demonstrates that happiness is not something money can simply buy; it depends on deeper, [[non-material]] [[fulfilment]].
fixes.why: 'buy' is plain; marked 'diminishing returns' and the full word 'non-material'

fixes.answer: Our environment has a [[profound influence]] on our wellbeing. A supportive community, safe and pleasant surroundings, and access to nature and green space all contribute significantly to happiness. Conversely, a stressful, [[isolating]] or polluted environment can seriously [[undermine]] it. The people around us, our relationships and social connections, are perhaps the most important environmental factor of all. So happiness is not purely internal; it is profoundly shaped by our surroundings and relationships.

I am genuinely uncertain. On one hand, advances in medicine, technology and [[living standards]] could improve wellbeing. There is also growing awareness of mental health and the importance of a balanced life. On the other hand, rising pressures, social media comparison and uncertainty could work against happiness. So I think future happiness will depend less on material progress and more on whether we learn to [[prioritise]] the things that genuinely [[nourish]] human wellbeing.

Societies can take meaningful steps. Prioritising mental health services and reducing the [[stigma]] around them is crucial. Fostering community, reducing inequality, and ensuring people have access to nature, leisure and a healthy work-life balance all help. Some argue governments should measure national wellbeing, not just economic output. Essentially, by valuing human [[flourishing]] alongside economic growth, societies can create conditions in which more people can genuinely [[thrive]] and feel content.

This is quite paradoxical. Striving for a good, meaningful life is clearly positive. However, obsessively pursuing happiness as a goal in itself can be [[counterproductive]]; it can create pressure and dissatisfaction when we inevitably experience negative emotions, which are a normal part of life. Chasing constant positivity is unrealistic. So I would argue that accepting the full range of human emotions and finding meaning is healthier than a relentless, anxious [[pursuit]] of [[fleeting]] pleasure.

I partly agree, but with important reservations. There is real truth that our attitude, gratitude and how we respond to circumstances significantly influence our happiness, so mindset matters. However, saying happiness is simply a choice can be [[dismissive]] of those facing genuine hardship, mental illness or difficult circumstances beyond their control. So while we have some agency over our happiness, I think it is [[oversimplified]] to call it purely a choice, ignoring the [[structural]] and biological factors involved.
